title: Floating Point with SSE
summary: x64 code does floating-point maths in the 16 **xmm** registers with **SSE** instructions. Scalar instructions like `addss` work on one `float`; packed ones like `addps` work on four at once, the start of **SIMD**. This lesson reads typical game maths in assembly: loading constants, arithmetic, comparisons, conversions between ints and floats, and a first look at vectorised code.
markdown:
## The xmm registers

Each `xmm0` to `xmm15` register is 128 bits wide: room for four `float`s or two `double`s. (Newer processors extend them to 256-bit `ymm` and 512-bit `zmm` registers with AVX; the ideas are the same.)

For ordinary scalar maths the compiler uses only the lowest lane:

```
xmm0:  [ float 3 | float 2 | float 1 | float 0 ]     <- scalar code uses lane 0 only
        127                               31   0
```

Instruction names end in a suffix saying what they work on:

| Suffix | Means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `ss` | **S**calar **S**ingle: one `float` | `addss xmm0, xmm1` |
| `sd` | **S**calar **D**ouble: one `double` | `mulsd xmm0, xmm2` |
| `ps` | **P**acked **S**ingle: four `float`s | `addps xmm0, xmm1` |
| `pd` | **P**acked **D**ouble: two `double`s | `subpd xmm3, xmm4` |

## Everyday float code

```cpp
float speedAfterFriction(float speed, float friction, float dt)
{
    return speed * (1.0f - friction * dt);
}
```

```asm
speedAfterFriction PROC
    mulss  xmm1, xmm2                          ; friction * dt
    movss  xmm3, dword ptr [__real@3f800000]   ; load the constant 1.0f
    subss  xmm3, xmm1                          ; 1.0f - friction*dt
    mulss  xmm0, xmm3                          ; speed * (...)
    ret                                        ; result in xmm0
speedAfterFriction ENDP
```

- Arguments arrive in `xmm0`, `xmm1`, `xmm2` by position (lesson 7.06); the result leaves in `xmm0`.
- There are no float immediates: constants live in read-only data and are loaded from memory. MSVC names them after their bits, so `__real@3f800000` is 1.0f (lesson 2.11's table). Reading those names tells you the constants directly.
- `movss` loads and stores one float; `movaps`/`movups` move all 128 bits (aligned or unaligned).

## Conversions and comparisons

| Instruction | Does | C++ |
|---|---|---|
| `cvtsi2ss xmm0, eax` | int to float | `static_cast<float>(i)` |
| `cvttss2si eax, xmm0` | float to int, truncating towards zero | `static_cast<int>(f)` |
| `cvtss2sd xmm0, xmm0` | float to double | passing a `float` to `printf` |
| `comiss xmm0, xmm1` / `ucomiss` | compare, setting ZF, CF (and PF) | `a < b` |
| `sqrtss`, `minss`, `maxss` | square root, minimum, maximum | `std::sqrt`, `std::min` |
| `xorps xmm0, xmm0` | zero the register | `0.0f` |

Float comparisons set the flags like an **unsigned** integer compare, so they are followed by `ja`, `jb`, `jae`, `jbe`, not `jg`/`jl`. Comparisons involving NaN ("not a number") are "unordered" and set the parity flag, which is why you sometimes see an extra `jp` after them.

## SIMD: four at once

The packed instructions do the same operation on every lane in one go. Adding two arrays of floats four elements per instruction is up to four times the work per instruction:

```asm
top:
    movups xmm0, [rcx+rax]       ; load 4 floats from a
    movups xmm1, [rdx+rax]       ; load 4 floats from b
    addps  xmm0, xmm1            ; 4 additions in one instruction
    movups [r8+rax], xmm0        ; store 4 results
    add    rax, 16               ; advance by 4 floats
    cmp    rax, r9
    jb     top
```

Optimising compilers produce loops like this automatically from plain C++ (**auto-vectorisation**) when the loop is simple enough: no dependencies between iterations, no function calls in the body, data laid out contiguously. That last condition is a big part of why engines store data as **structures of arrays** (all x values together, all y values together) rather than arrays of structures for the hottest loops. You can also write SIMD by hand with **intrinsics** (`_mm_add_ps` and friends from `<immintrin.h>`), which map one-to-one onto these instructions.

## Precision and determinism

`float` has about 7 significant decimal digits; `double` about 16. Results can differ with optimisation settings (the compiler may reorder `a + b + c` only under `/fp:fast`, which is not the default) and between processors for some library functions. For lockstep multiplayer games and replays, which need bit-identical results everywhere, programs keep the default `/fp:precise`, avoid `/fp:fast`, and sometimes use fixed-point integers for game logic instead.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Expecting float arguments in rcx/rdx
> Floating-point arguments use the `xmm` register of their position.

> [!warning] Reading a float comparison's `ja` as unsigned integers
> After `comiss`, `ja`/`jb` are simply "greater"/"less" for floats.

> [!warning] Converting with truncation when rounding was meant
> `static_cast<int>(2.9f)` is 2. Use `std::lround` to round.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What do the suffixes `ss`, `sd`, `ps` and `pd` mean?
- Signed short, signed double, positive single, positive double
+ Scalar single, scalar double, packed single (four floats), packed double (two doubles)
- Single step, single double, page single, page double
- Short store, short double, packed store, packed double
> `addss` adds one float; `addps` adds four floats at once.

? Where do a function's float arguments and float result go on x64 Windows?
- On the stack, with the result in `rax`
- In `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, with the result in `xmm0`
- In the x87 floating-point stack
+ The first four arguments in `xmm0` to `xmm3` by position; the result in `xmm0`
> Integer results come back in `rax`; float and double results come back in `xmm0`.

? What does a loop need for the compiler to vectorise it?
- A `#pragma` on every line of the body
+ Independent iterations, a simple body and contiguous data
- A loop counter of type `float`
- At least a million iterations
> Then several elements can be processed per instruction, four floats at a time with SSE.

? What does `mulss xmm0, xmm1` do?
- Multiplies four floats in each register
+ Multiplies the lowest float of xmm0 by xmm1's
- Multiplies two doubles
> `ss` means scalar single precision.

? Why does compiled float code load constants from memory?
- Constants are faster from memory
- The compiler cannot compute them
+ x64 instructions cannot hold floating-point immediates
> They are stored in read-only data, often named after their bit pattern.

? What is the advantage of `addps` over `addss`?
+ It adds four pairs of floats in one instruction
- It is more precise
- It works with integers
> Packed instructions operate on every lane at once: SIMD.

? After `comiss xmm0, xmm1`, which jump means "xmm0 is greater"?
- `jg`
+ `ja`
- `jl`
> Float compares set the flags like an unsigned comparison.
```
ideas:
- Compile `speedAfterFriction` with `/O2 /FA` and decode each `__real@` constant's name with lesson 2.11's table.
- Write a loop adding two `std::vector<float>`s element by element and look for `addps` in the optimised output. Then add a `std::cout` inside the loop and look again.
- In the debugger's Registers window, right-click and enable the SSE registers, and watch `xmm0` while stepping float code.
